summary.oneLiner: eMudhra is a global digital trust platform company offering digital identity, e-signature, PKI/certificate authority, certificate lifecycle management and identity & access management solutions to enterprises and governments.
summary.business: eMudhra Limited is a licensed Certifying Authority (since 2008) that provides end-to-end digital trust services spanning eSignatures (emSigner), Certificate Lifecycle Management (CertiNext), a global Certificate Authority/PKI platform (emCA), and converged Identity & Access Management (SecurePass), serving enterprises, governments and channel partners. It serves customers across banking, government, defence, telecommunications, healthcare and manufacturing in 35+ countries, and in FY26 expanded into Europe via the Cryptas acquisition and into Central Asia via a new Almaty office.

currentContext.strengths: Issued 100 million+ digital certificates cumulatively, positioning it as the largest DSC issuer in India|Unified, end-to-end Digital Trust Platform spanning eSignatures, PKI/CA, Certificate Lifecycle Management and IAM under one integrated stack, sharpening competitive differentiation|Global footprint across 35+ countries with regional delivery centres in Asia, Europe, the Middle East and the Americas, and 1000+ enterprise customers plus 100K+ channel partners|Early mover in post-quantum cryptography readiness (emCA prepared for post-quantum era) and agentic-AI trust infrastructure|Intellectual/policy leadership in digital trust and Digital Public Infrastructure discourse, reinforcing credibility with governments and regulators|Extensive India distribution network of Chartered Accountants and Company Secretaries used to reach SMEs (e.g., emSigner for SMEs)
currentContext.strategies: Consolidate standalone products (emCA, CertiNext, SecurePass, emSigner) into a single, cohesive, integrated Digital Trust Platform rather than separately licensed point products|Continue geographic expansion into new regions — completed formal entry into Europe via the Cryptas acquisition and into Central Asia via a new Almaty (Kazakhstan) office|Build post-quantum and crypto-agile engineering into the stack (emCA, CertiNext, emSigner, SecurePass) so customers can run classical and post-quantum cryptography in parallel during transition|Democratise enterprise-grade digital signing for India's SME segment via emSigner for SMEs, distributed through the company's network of Chartered Accountants and Company Secretaries|Build dedicated trust infrastructure for autonomous/agentic AI systems (authentication, behaviour governance, real-time credential revocation)|Engineer privacy-by-design capability (data discovery and management platform) as a product feature rather than a policy document, covering consent capture, purpose binding and cross-border transfer governance|Sustain thought leadership and policy engagement on digital trust as foundational to Digital Public Infrastructure and the AI economy|The Notice of AGM includes a resolution to declare a dividend on equity shares for FY 2025-26, indicating an intent to pay dividends; no explicit payout-ratio policy, buyback or debt-reduction philosophy is disclosed in the text provided. Related-party investments made by the listed entity are stated as 100% concentrated in related parties (BRSR 'Openness of business' disclosure), a structural/relationship fact rather than a capital-allocation policy statement.
currentContext.expansion: eMudhra's FY26 expansion was geographic and product-platform led rather than physical-capacity led (asset-light IT/digital-trust business). It acquired Cryptas, a Europe-headquartered digital trust and PKI solutions provider, marking formal entry into the European market and extending its footprint from the Americas and Asia-Pacific, through the Middle East and Africa, into Europe. It also opened a new office in Almaty, Kazakhstan, marking entry into Central Asia, and obtained MOSIP certification enabling it to power population-scale digital identity infrastructure across Africa. On the product side, it launched emSigner for SMEs (distributed through its network of Chartered Accountants and Company Secretaries) and, during the year, introduced a data discovery and management platform and a federated identity orchestration platform (ID Broker) as new platform capabilities.
currentContext.mdna: Post-quantum cryptography moving from standard to mandate (NIST FIPS 203/204/205; US CNSA 2.0 phased deadlines through 2030-2035) is expected to drive enterprise and government demand for crypto-agile trust infrastructure|Phased data-privacy regulation coming into force — India's Digital Personal Data Protection Rules (notified 13 Nov 2025, phased through 13 May 2027), EU eIDAS 2.0 (EUDI Wallet deadline 31 Dec 2026), NIS2 and DORA — is expanding enterprise cybersecurity/compliance obligations that management frames as a demand driver|Collapsing public TLS certificate lifetimes (CA/Browser Forum SC-081v3: 200 days from March 2026, 100 days from March 2027, 47 days from March 2029) is making manual certificate management unviable, favouring automated certificate lifecycle management platforms like CertiNext|Proliferation of autonomous AI agents that transact, sign and access systems is shifting demand toward authenticating and governing AI agents in real time, a new opportunity area the company is targeting|National-scale digitalisation programmes in emerging markets (e.g., MOSIP-enabled population-scale digital identity in Africa; Central Asia's digitalisation push) are cited as opportunities for the company's trust infrastructure

risks.risk: Licence and accreditation dependency: the business runs on retaining its Certifying Authority licence in India and other geographies, ongoing WebTrust accreditation, compliance with CA/Browser Forum requirements, and continued acceptance of eMudhra's Root Certificate by the browsers
risks.note: The AR's legal/regulatory risk row names 'inability to comply with changes in guidelines, audit requirements or maintain its license in India or other geographies' as a key risk. Root-certificate acceptance by browsers is a third-party gate the company does not control, and losing it would stop the issuance of SSL certificates outright - this is an existence-level dependency rather than a margin risk.

risks.risk: Privacy-regulation and data-localisation exposure - verification, storage and processing of identity data forces ongoing GDPR/DPDP-type compliance, plus local data storage mandates for trust services in geographies such as the European Union and Indonesia
risks.note: Flagged twice: as a legal/regulatory risk ('inability to comply on an ongoing basis with privacy guidelines such as GDPR', 'local data storage requirements... European Union, Indonesia etc.') and as BRSR material issue no. 2, Privacy and Data Security, rated both Opportunity and Risk. Localisation requirements are a structural cost driver because they force in-country infrastructure per geography rather than a single shared platform.

risks.risk: Regulatory-adoption dependency: insufficient regulatory push, adverse changes to the Electronic Transactions Act, or lack of relying-party adoption of digital signature certificates by Governments, Banks and other relying parties
risks.note: Demand is created by statute, not by the company - the AR grounds acceptance in the UNCITRAL Model Law on eSignatures 2000 as incorporated into national Electronic Transactions Act / Information Technology Act regimes. A structural risk because revenue depends on legislatures and on relying parties choosing to honour certificates, and the mitigation offered is only that the technology has been accepted for >20 years and that eMudhra participates in global standards bodies.

risks.risk: Contractual liability, indemnity and SLA exposure on enterprise contracts, including litigation or requests for evidence arising from mis-use of a digital signature
risks.note: The AR states eMudhra is bound by obligations for timely delivery, SLA fulfilment, IP infringement protection and confidentiality, and that material breach 'typically triggers service credits, liability and indemnity cover'. Mitigation is a stated cap: liabilities limited to actual damages with an indemnity cap of the previous 12 months' fee received from the client - but with carve-outs for IP infringement, confidentiality, gross negligence and wilful misconduct, which are precisely the uncapped tail scenarios.

risks.risk: Foreign-exchange risk on 64% of FY2025-26 revenue earned from international operations, realised in USD, EUR, AED and other currencies against a largely INR cost base
risks.note: The company's own figure. Adverse currency movement against the INR lowers realisation while 'substantial costs are incurred' in rupees, so the exposure is a translation-and-margin risk, not a hedged trading exposure - the stated mitigation is only regular transfer pricing of FX collections and repatriation to India to shorten the exposure window, with no hedging programme disclosed.

risks.risk: Receivables and counterparty-recovery risk - unsecured credit extended to partners and customers, including sectors in emerging-market countries described by the company as risky from a payment-recoverability standpoint
risks.note: Listed first under Financial and Compliance Risk as affecting 'ability to maintain profitability and cash flows'; the AR states non-recoverability results in provisioning in P/L. Credit is extended on the basis of history of association rather than security, so growth into new emerging-market geographies structurally raises the provisioning risk.

risks.risk: Talent dependency and elevated attrition - permanent-employee turnover rose to 35.20% in FY2025-26 from 26.56% in FY2024-25, with female attrition at 47.22%
risks.note: The BRSR turnover table quantifies what the Human Resource Risk section describes qualitatively: as a technology-focused company eMudhra is 'dependent heavily on its people' for building, delivering and supporting products, and BRSR material issue no. 3 notes market demand for skilled talent is high. Attrition up ~9 points year-on-year on a knowledge business is a direct delivery and cost risk; mitigation cited is continuous re-skilling plus automating and streamlining processes.

risks.risk: Operations risk across identity verification, customer support and internal IT - incorrect interpretation of vetting guidelines can cause audit violations, poor support of a large retail and partner base creates brand, reputation and renewal risk, and IT mismanagement can cause service disruption
risks.note: The AR's Operations Risk row splits operations into identity verification, customer support and IT operations and ties each to a specific failure mode. Audit violations matter disproportionately here because the licence and WebTrust accreditation in risk 1 depend on clean audits - the company notes it 'has had clean audits from the beginning of its operations', which makes that record itself a load-bearing asset.

one-line thesis: eMudhra delivered strong FY26 product-led growth (35% revenue, 26% PAT) driven by global PKI demand and the Cryptas acquisition, with management guiding for sustained 18% organic top-line and ~28% bottom-line expansion in FY27 fueled by margin-accretive enterprise software mix shift.
financial scorecard: Revenue: INR 7,132mn (+35% YoY); EBITDA: INR 1,654mn (+33% YoY, 23.2% margin); PAT: INR 1,100mn (+26% YoY, 15.4% margin); Order Book: INR 2,380mn (Product-only, ~2.3x forward coverage); Net Debt: Not explicitly stated but capex focused on DC expansion; One-offs: Cryptas integration costs largely absorbed, now breakeven/profitable.
guidance: Revenue growth: ~18% organic (Total ~18% as no major M&A planned); Margin: PAT growth 25-30% (driven by product mix); Order inflow: Strong pipeline in US/EU/Africa; Capex: Continued investment in US/EU/India data centers for sovereignty.
order book & pipeline: INR 238 crores (exclusively product business); Management projects 2.2x-2.3x conversion to next year revenue despite some Middle East delays due to geopolitical tensions.
segment / subsidiary detail: Enterprise Solutions: 59% of rev, +55% YoY (23% organic, 32% acquisitive); Trust Services: 20% of rev, +32% YoY (driven by combo certs/tokens); Pure Services: 21% of rev, flat YoY.
growth verticals / optionality: US University Federation (InCommon) win providing visibility across 700 institutions; PQC mandates (2029-30) creating early POCs in BFSI/Defense; Africa DPI stack deployments; Cross-selling CertiNext into Cryptas EU base.
margins & cost dynamics: PAT margin expansion driven by shift to high-gross-margin Enterprise Products vs flat low-margin Services; Cryptas expected to contribute >$1mn profit in FY27 as US CLM solutions are replaced with eMudhra's stack.
capex / expansion: Strategic capex in multi-region data centers (US, Europe, UAE, India) to meet data sovereignty laws; R&D spend on Agentic AI layers and Post-Quantum Cryptography.
capital allocation: Open to selective bolt-on acquisitions in US focused on AI-based cybersecurity/identity capabilities; No active pipeline currently; Focus on organic scaling to double PAT in 3 years.
risks & watch-items: Geopolitical delays in Middle East orders; Google Root Certificate policy transitions (managed but ongoing); Long sales cycles in European banking sector; Competitive threat from foundational AI models identifying vulnerabilities (mitigated by increased security spend).
management quality / tone: Confident and disciplined; Emphasizes 100% track record on guidance achievement; Cautious on M&A (waiting for right AI targets); Transparent on India Q4 volatility due to high base/defense deal timing.
non-obvious takeaways: Management explicitly clarifies that AI models (like 'Mythos'/Claude) expand the attack surface rather than replacing security vendors, forcing enterprises (e.g., public sector banks) to increase security budgets by ~50%; Cryptas integration profitability hinges on swapping out American CLM competitors within their existing client base.

themes.title: Digital platforms, SaaS, payments & cybersecurity
themes.need: Digital-public-infrastructure scale, enterprise SaaS and a compliance/security upcycle drive a distinct platform cohort. PINELABS/NPST/CMSINFO on payments; AURIONPRO/NEWGEN/NUCLEUS/ROUTE/TANLA on banking/CPaaS software; EMUDHRA/META(544441)/AURIONPRO on digital-identity & cybersecurity; CAPILLARY/MAPMYINDIA/NAZARA on SaaS/geospatial/gaming. Q1FY27 anchored the payments leg: PAYTM's GMV grew 31% YoY (accelerating 23% -> 27% -> 31%) with merchant payments about 80% of the financial-services mix and 25-30 lakh device additions a year on a distribution-only lending model (no book, no FLDG); MOBIKWIK posted payments GMV of INR 52,400cr (+58% YoY), a 13th consecutive record quarter and India's largest wallet by GTV at ~20% share, against only ~INR 3,200cr of digital-credit GMV. OFSS adds the banking-software annuity, with RPO +17% YoY versus revenue +7% and licence-and-cloud revenue +13% at a 44% operating margin.
themes.driver: Deal/ARR additions; festive digital-payments TPV; merchant-device additions; RBI/regulatory compliance-driven security spend.
